findings.source_quote: καὶ ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἔστι πιστεῦσαι, ἢ καὶ ὁ ἀὴρ
findings.english_quote: And this is all the more credible, since even the air
findings.issue: The draft converts the printed connection into an explicit causal assertion. In the supplied wording, μᾶλλον followed by ἢ supports a comparison; ἢ does not itself mean “since.” The note acknowledges the comparative alternative, but that disclosure does not establish the causal wording in the main text.
findings.suggested_revision: Test a comparative rendering such as “And this is more readily believable than even that the air …,” continuing with the surviving account of the air’s transformations. Explain the contextual difficulty in a note without replacing the printed ἢ with an unprinted causal or relative conjunction. This is a translation issue in the verified print, not grounds for alleging an OCR error.

findings.source_quote: καὶ ὁμοούσιον μὴ παρούσῃ τροπῇ προβάλλει, ἰσοδύναμον δὲ οὔ
findings.english_quote: and through a transformation not already present it brings forth something of the same substance, though not equal in power.
findings.issue: “Already” supplies an unsupported temporal qualification. Moreover, the draft presents the transformation as the instrument of projection without disclosing the materially different circumstantial reading of μὴ παρούσῃ τροπῇ: a transformation is not present or taking place. The difference concerns whether projection involves a new transformation or occurs without an accompanying transformation.
findings.suggested_revision: Remove “already.” Evaluate the proposed wording “and brings forth something of the same substance, without a transformation being present, but not equal in power.” If adopting that circumstantial reading, explain it and preserve the instrumental alternative, “by a transformation that is not present,” in a source-quoted note. The revised wording requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ὁ δὲ προβληθεὶς τῆς ἐξ ἐκείνου τροπῆς τε καὶ τέκνον ὑπάρχων
findings.english_quote: whereas the one brought forth, being both a transformation derived from him and his child
findings.issue: The draft makes the projected being itself a transformation. The supplied τροπῆς is genitive, not a nominative predicate identifying that being as a transformation. Its attachment may be debated, but the existing note does not explain a grammatical basis for the identity claim or preserve the viable genitive attachments.
findings.suggested_revision: Use a rendering that retains the genitive relationship, for example “whereas the one brought forth, being also a child of the transformation originating from that one ….” Explain the alternative attachment in which the genitive expresses the projected being’s origin and “child” is a further description. Do not retain “being both a transformation … and his child” merely by labeling the coordination awkward.

findings.source_quote: ἔξω δὲ αὐτῆς κατὰ τὴν τοῦ προβαλόντος βουλὴν κραθείσης πρὸς τὴν κρᾶσιν ἡ κακοῖς χαίρουσα προαίρεσις
findings.english_quote: but when substance outside it had been mixed into the mixture in accordance with the will of the one who brought it forth, the disposition that delights in evils arose.
findings.issue: The draft introduces a separate substance situated outside the fourfold substance. A natural construction instead takes αὐτῆς as the subject of the genitive absolute κραθείσης, referring back to the already mentioned substance, with ἔξω modifying its external mixing. The following reference to “the substance mixed externally by him” supports considering that construction. The draft neither establishes its supplied second substance nor discloses this consequential attachment and referent choice.
findings.suggested_revision: Test “but when that substance had been mixed externally according to the will of the one who brought it forth, the disposition that delights in evils arose in connection with the mixture.” Preserve the attachment uncertainty in a source-quoted note, including the alternative treatment of ἔξω αὐτῆς. Do not assert an additional material constituent without a defensible account of the supplied syntax.

findings.issue: Although the five printed dots remain visible, “You have” supplies a second-person active construction that the surviving verbal beginning εἴρ does not establish. The unavailable ending could distinguish constructions such as an active address and a passive statement that everything has been said correctly. The source note’s assertion that no missing ending has been supplied overlooks the grammatical information supplied in English. The block concerns unsupported completion of unavailable meaning, not the mere existence of a confirmed printed lacuna.
findings.suggested_revision: Retain “everything” and “correctly,” but represent the surviving saying-verb fragment without supplying its unavailable person and voice. One possible explicitly fragmentary presentation is “Everything correctly—εἴρ.....,” with a source-quoted note explaining the recognizable saying-verb beginning, the five-dot printed gap, and the absence of any restoration. Alternatively, develop an equally explicit English fragment for fresh review. Further print verification is not required merely to confirm this already image-checked gap.

findings.english_quote: Peter is understood as the unexpressed object.
findings.issue: The main English sentence correctly identifies Peter as the recipient of the blessing, but this lexical note inaccurately calls the object unexpressed. The accusative participle εἰπόντα supplies the object description: the one who had said these things.
findings.suggested_revision: Revise the note to state that Peter is the contextual referent of the accusative εἰπόντα, “him who had said these things,” which functions as the object of εὐλογήσαμεν. The main sentence need not change on this account.
